hypotheses.title: sync_ledger callable by anyone to inflate/deflate arbitrary user balances
hypotheses.description: sync_ledger() has no access control and trusts msg.sender as the lending market. Any external caller can invoke it directly, and since lendingMarket = msg.sender, the whitelist check in update_market() will only pass if the caller is a whitelisted market. However, the function also accepts an arbitrary _lender and _delta, so any whitelisted market (or a contract that is whitelisted) can arbitrarily credit/debit any user's amount and rewardDebt. More critically, if a market is whitelisted, anyone calling through that market's context can manipulate user accounting.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker identifies a whitelisted lending market address. 2) Attacker calls sync_ledger(victim, +hugeDelta) directly from that market's address (or via a market that forwards calls). 3) user.amount and rewardDebt are inflated. 4) Attacker (or victim) claims inflated CANTO rewards via claim().
hypotheses.impact: Theft of CANTO rewards from the LendingLedger contract; incorrect accounting of user balances and market totals; potential insolvency of the reward pool.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict sync_ledger to be callable only by the registered lending market (or its liquidity gauge), e.g., require(msg.sender == market || msg.sender == liquidityGauges[market]).

hypotheses.title: GaugeController.vote_for_gauge_weights uses stale user slope
hypotheses.description: The function reads `ve.getLastUserPoint(msg.sender)` to obtain `slope_`, but `getLastUserPoint` returns the last checkpointed point without extrapolating to the current block. If the user's lock has been decaying (bias decreasing) since the last checkpoint, the returned slope is stale and does not reflect the current voting power. The code then computes `new_slope.slope = (slope * _user_weight) / 10_000` using this stale slope, and `new_bias = new_slope.slope * new_dt`. Because the slope is stale, the recorded vote weight can be higher than the user's actual current voting power, allowing over-voting.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker creates a lock with a large amount, checkpoints it (slope recorded). 2) Attacker waits for time to pass without any checkpoint (slope decays in reality but `getLastUserPoint` still returns the old slope). 3) Attacker calls `vote_for_gauge_weights` with `_user_weight = 10000`, using the stale (higher) slope to compute `new_slope.slope`. 4) The gauge weight is inflated relative to the attacker's true current voting power. 5) Attacker repeats across gauges or uses the inflated weight to capture disproportionate rewards.
hypotheses.impact: Vote weight inflation; attacker captures more gauge rewards than deserved, diluting honest voters and potentially draining reward pools.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `ve.balanceOf(msg.sender)` (which extrapolates to current time) or explicitly checkpoint the user before reading the slope.

hypotheses.title: VotingEscrow.withdraw underflows delegated when lock was delegated
hypotheses.description: `withdraw` requires `locked_.delegatee == msg.sender`, so a delegated lock cannot be withdrawn by the delegatee. However, `newLocked.delegated -= int128(int256(amountToSend))` subtracts the full `amount` from `delegated`. If the user previously delegated part of their voting power to another address via `DELEGATE` action (which increases the delegatee's `delegated` but not the delegator's), the delegator's own `delegated` may be less than `amount`, causing an underflow revert. More critically, in `increaseAmount` when `delegatee != msg.sender`, the sender's `newLocked.delegated` is NOT increased (only `amount`), but the delegatee's `delegated` is increased. When the sender later withdraws, `newLocked.delegated -= amountToSend` underflows because `delegated < amount`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker creates a lock of X. 2) Attacker delegates to address B via `DELEGATE` (or `increaseAmount` while delegated). 3) Attacker's `locked.delegated` is now less than `locked.amount`. 4) Attacker calls `withdraw()` after lock expiry — the subtraction `newLocked.delegated -= amountToSend` underflows and reverts, permanently freezing the attacker's funds (or, if it doesn't revert due to int128 wrap, corrupts accounting).
hypotheses.impact: Frozen funds — the user cannot withdraw their locked CANTO. Alternatively, if the subtraction wraps, the global slope accounting is corrupted.
hypotheses.recommendation: Set `newLocked.delegated = 0` on withdraw (as done for `delegatee`), or track delegated amounts separately from `amount`.

hypotheses.title: LendingLedger.claim sends CANTO before updating reward state via callback
hypotheses.description: `claim()` computes `cantoToSend`, updates `user.rewardDebt = accumulatedCanto`, then makes an external `msg.sender.call{value: cantoToSend}("")`. Because the native CANTO transfer invokes the recipient's `receive()`/`fallback()`, an attacker contract can re-enter `claim()` before the function returns. The `rewardDebt` has been updated to `accumulatedCanto`, so `cantoToSend` on re-entry is zero — but the attacker can instead re-enter `update_market` or `sync_ledger` paths, or call `claim` across multiple markets. More critically, the lack of a reentrancy guard combined with `update_market` being callable by anyone allows state manipulation mid-call.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a contract with a `receive()` that re-calls `claim(_market)` (harmless here, zero payout) or calls `update_market(_otherMarket)` and then `claim(_otherMarket)`. 2) Attacker calls `claim(marketA)`; during the external call, re-enters `claim(marketB)`. 3) If `marketB`'s `update_market` was stale, re-entrant call recomputes and pays out using state not yet settled for `marketA`. Repeat across many markets in a single transaction.
hypotheses.impact: Cross-market/self reentrancy enabling multiple payouts of CANTO rewards in a single tx, potentially draining the contract's CANTO balance faster than accounting permits.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `nonReentrant` to `claim`, `sync_ledger`, and `update_market`, or follow strict checks-effects-interactions by zeroing/updating all reward state before the external call.

hypotheses.title: LendingLedger.sync_ledger trusts caller-supplied delta without market validation
hypotheses.description: `sync_ledger` is callable by any address that is whitelisted as a lending market (or its liquidity gauge). The function trusts the `_delta` parameter entirely and updates `user.amount`, `rewardDebt`, and `lendingMarketTotalBalance` accordingly. A malicious or compromised whitelisted market can call `sync_ledger` with arbitrary positive deltas for any `_lender`, inflating that lender's `amount` and enabling them to claim disproportionate CANTO rewards. Since `liquidityGauges` mapping is two-way, a gauge can also call with arbitrary deltas.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker gets a market whitelisted (or exploits an existing whitelisted market they control). 2) Attacker calls `sync_ledger(victimOrSelf, hugePositiveDelta)` to inflate `user.amount`. 3) Attacker calls `claim(market)` to drain CANTO rewards proportional to the inflated amount. 4) Attacker calls `sync_ledger(self, -hugeDelta)` to restore balance and avoid detection.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of CANTO rewards from LendingLedger, draining funds meant for legitimate lenders.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `sync_ledger` to only be callable by the market itself (msg.sender == market) and validate that the delta corresponds to actual token movements, or use a pull-based accounting model.

hypotheses.title: sync_ledger uses gauge address as market key, breaking reward accounting
hypotheses.description: When a liquidity gauge exists for a market, sync_ledger() replaces `lendingMarket` with the gauge address and then reads/writes `marketInfo[lendingMarket]`, `userInfo[lendingMarket][_lender]`, and `lendingMarketTotalBalance[lendingMarket]` using the gauge address. However, `update_market` and `claim` operate on the market address, and `whiteListLendingMarket` initializes `marketInfo[_market]` (the market, not the gauge). This mismatch means gauge-based deposits accrue rewards against a different accumulator than the one `claim` reads, and `lendingMarketTotalBalance` is split between two keys.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Governance whitelists a market with a gauge (trusted setup, but the flaw is in the untrusted user path). 2) A user deposits via LiquidityGauge.depositUnderlying, which calls sync_ledger with the gauge as msg.sender. 3) sync_ledger remaps to the gauge address and updates `userInfo[gauge][user]` and `lendingMarketTotalBalance[gauge]`. 4) When the user calls claim(market), it reads `userInfo[market][user]` (zero) and `marketInfo[market]`, so the user either receives nothing or the accounting is inconsistent. 5) Conversely, a user who deposits directly to the market can claim against a total balance that excludes gauge deposits, over-paying relative to actual supply.
hypotheses.impact: Rewards are misallocated: some users cannot claim accrued CANTO (frozen rewards), while others can claim more than their fair share, potentially draining the LendingLedger's CANTO balance and causing insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: In sync_ledger, keep the market address as the accounting key and only use the gauge for the whitelist check; or consistently use the gauge address in update_market, claim, and whiteListLendingMarket.

hypotheses.title: LiquidityGauge._afterTokenTransfer double-counts on transfer
hypotheses.description: On every ERC20 transfer, _afterTokenTransfer calls sync_ledger(from, -amount) and sync_ledger(to, +amount). However, sync_ledger is invoked with msg.sender being the LiquidityGauge, and LendingLedger.sync_ledger maps msg.sender through liquidityGauges[lendingMarket] to the underlying market. This means the gauge's own balance in the ledger is never tracked; instead the ledger updates the underlying market's userInfo for the from/to addresses. Combined with depositUnderlying/withdrawUnderlying which do NOT call sync_ledger, the ledger's accounting for the gauge is inconsistent: deposits via depositUnderlying never credit the user in the ledger, while transfers do. Users can transfer gauge tokens to themselves or others to inflate ledger balances without depositing underlying.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls depositUnderlying(amount) — ledger is not updated (no sync_ledger call). 2) Attacker transfers gauge tokens to a fresh address; _afterTokenTransfer calls sync_ledger(to, +amount), crediting the fresh address in the ledger. 3) Attacker calls claim() from the fresh address to receive CANTO rewards for tokens that were never properly accounted. 4) Attacker can also transfer back and forth to repeatedly credit balances.
hypotheses.impact: Inflated user.amount in LendingLedger leading to over-claiming of CANTO rewards and eventual insolvency of the reward pool.
hypotheses.recommendation: Call sync_ledger in depositUnderlying/withdrawUnderlying and ensure _afterTokenTransfer does not double-count; or remove sync_ledger from _afterTokenTransfer and only sync on deposit/withdraw.

hypotheses.title: claim() can be called by anyone for any market, draining rewards to caller
hypotheses.description: claim(address _market) is external with no access control and uses msg.sender as the beneficiary. Any untrusted actor can call claim() for any whitelisted market. If the caller has a nonzero user.amount in that market (e.g., via a liquidity gauge or by being a lender), they can drain accumulated CANTO. More importantly, because sync_ledger is also unauthenticated, an attacker can first inflate their own user.amount via a whitelisted market, then call claim() to extract CANTO.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls sync_ledger(attacker, +largeDelta) through a whitelisted market context. 2) Attacker calls claim(market). 3) accumulatedCanto is computed from inflated user.amount, and cantoToSend is sent to attacker.
hypotheses.impact: Direct loss of CANTO funds held by LendingLedger; reward pool drained.
hypotheses.recommendation: Ensure sync_ledger is properly access-controlled so user.amount cannot be inflated; claim() itself is fine if accounting is sound.

hypotheses.title: LiquidityGauge._afterTokenTransfer trusts arbitrary lendingLedger caller
hypotheses.description: _afterTokenTransfer calls LendingLedger(lendingLedger).sync_ledger(from/to, ±amount) on every transfer, including transfers initiated by any holder. Since sync_ledger has no access control, any user who holds gauge tokens can transfer them to manipulate the ledger. Additionally, the gauge's depositUnderlying/withdrawUnderlying mint/burn and trigger sync_ledger, but a user can also transfer gauge tokens to an arbitrary address to credit that address in the ledger without actually depositing underlying tokens.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker acquires a small amount of gauge tokens. 2) Attacker transfers them to a victim or to themselves repeatedly, each transfer calling sync_ledger with ±amount. 3) Because sync_ledger is unauthenticated, the attacker can also call it directly with arbitrary deltas. 4) Attacker claims inflated rewards.
hypotheses.impact: Reward accounting corruption; theft of CANTO from LendingLedger.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add access control to sync_ledger so only the gauge (or registered market) can call it, and ensure the gauge only reports actual deposit/withdraw events.

hypotheses.title: LendingLedger.claim uses stale accCantoPerShare for non-updated markets
hypotheses.description: `claim` calls `update_market(_market)` which only updates if `block.number > market.lastRewardBlock`. If `marketSupply == 0` at the time of update, `accCantoPerShare` is not incremented but `lastRewardBlock` is still set to `block.number`, permanently skipping rewards for that interval. When supply later becomes positive, those skipped rewards are lost to users. Additionally, `update_market` uses `gaugeController.gauge_relative_weight_write(_market, epochTime)` where `epochTime` is computed from `referenceBlockTime + (block.number - referenceBlockNumber) * averageBlockTime / 1000` — this is the *current* time, not the epoch time, so all epochs in the loop use the same relative weight, misallocating rewards across epochs.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A market has zero supply for a period. 2) `update_market` is called (e.g., by anyone via `sync_ledger` or `claim`), setting `lastRewardBlock = block.number` without accruing rewards. 3) Rewards for that period are permanently lost. Separately, an attacker can call `update_market` at a moment when the gauge weight is high to lock in a favorable `accCantoPerShare` for past epochs.
hypotheses.impact: Users receive incorrect reward amounts; rewards are permanently lost or misallocated across epochs.
hypotheses.recommendation: Only advance `lastRewardBlock` when `marketSupply > 0`, and compute `epochTime` per-epoch inside the loop rather than once from the current block.

hypotheses.title: LendingLedger uses manipulable averageBlockTime for epoch time
hypotheses.description: The `epochTime` used to query `gaugeController.gauge_relative_weight_write(_market, epochTime)` is derived from `referenceBlockTime + ((block.number - referenceBlockNumber) * averageBlockTime) / 1000`, where `averageBlockTime` is a governance-set constant (5700ms) that does not track actual block times. Because block production rate is not constant, the computed `epochTime` can drift arbitrarily far from the real wall-clock time, causing the gauge relative weight lookup to read the wrong weekly epoch's weight. An attacker who can influence block production timing (e.g., via MEV/block stuffing on Canto) can shift the effective epoch used for reward accrual.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes that `epochTime` is a linear function of block number with a fixed slope. 2) Attacker accelerates or delays block production around an epoch boundary (e.g., by spamming transactions to fill blocks or by exploiting validator timing) so that `epochTime` crosses a WEEK boundary at a different real time than intended. 3) `gauge_relative_weight_write` returns the weight for the wrong week, and `accCantoPerShare` is computed with that weight. 4) Attacker claims rewards at the inflated rate.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect reward distribution; attacker can extract more CANTO than entitled, draining the LendingLedger's CANTO balance and starving honest LPs.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `block.timestamp` directly for epoch time, or use a robust on-chain time oracle (e.g., Chainlink) instead of a governance-set average block time.

hypotheses.title: LendingLedger.claim lacks nonReentrant, allowing reentrancy via CANTO callback
hypotheses.description: `claim()` sends CANTO to `msg.sender` via a low-level `call` before the function returns, and the contract has no reentrancy guard. Although `user.rewardDebt` is updated before the send, the `update_market(_market)` call at the top of `claim()` recomputes `accCantoPerShare` based on `lendingMarketTotalBalance`, and a reentrant call can re-enter `claim()` while the outer call's state is partially consistent. More critically, `sync_ledger` is callable by any whitelisted market and can be invoked during the callback to manipulate `user.amount` and `rewardDebt` before the outer `claim` finishes, enabling double-claiming of rewards.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a malicious contract that is whitelisted as a lending market (or controls a whitelisted market's callback path). 2) Attacker calls `claim(market)` from a contract whose `receive()`/fallback re-enters `claim()` or `sync_ledger()`. 3) During the CANTO transfer callback, the attacker re-enters `claim()` to drain additional rewards before `rewardDebt` reflects the first payout, or calls `sync_ledger` to inflate `user.amount` and then claims again.
hypotheses.impact: Double-claiming of CANTO rewards, draining the LendingLedger's CANTO balance and causing insolvency for other users.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `nonReentrant` to `claim()` and `sync_ledger()`, and follow checks-effects-interactions strictly.

hypotheses.title: LiquidityGauge Gauge token transfer hooks trigger sync_ledger after burn/mint
hypotheses.description: `withdrawUnderlying` burns user gauge tokens (triggering `_afterTokenTransfer` → `LendingLedger.sync_ledger(from, -amount)`) and then transfers underlying ERC20 to the user. `_afterTokenTransfer` runs `sync_ledger` with a negative delta *before* the underlying token is transferred out. Since the ledger and ERC20 interactions occur in a single external call chain and ERC20 `_afterTokenTransfer` can be hooked by a malicious `to`/`from`, an attacker can reenter `LendingLedger.sync_ledger` or `update_market` in a state where their gauge balance is burned but the underlying token has not yet left the gauge contract.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker holds gauge tokens and calls `withdrawUnderlying(_amount)`. 2) `_burn` triggers `_afterTokenTransfer` → `sync_ledger(from, -amount)`. 3) If the underlying token or attacker-controlled hook reenters `sync_ledger(to, +amount)` on another account, or reenters `claim()`, ledger accounting can be manipulated before the underlying ERC20 leaves the gauge. 4) Because `sync_ledger` allows arbitrary callers (msg.sender gated only by `liquidityGauges` reverse mapping—which for the gauge IS itself), the attacker can perturbed market totals.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong reward-debt accounting in LendingLedger, potential for over-claiming CANTO rewards, and market balance underflow across reentrant sequences.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a reentrancy guard to LiquidityGauge deposit/withdraw and to LendingLedger.sync_ledger, or push sync_ledger updates atomically after all token movements and settle in one path.

hypotheses.title: LendingLedger.update_market unbounded while loop over blocks
hypotheses.description: `update_market` loops `while (i < block.number)` iterating in BLOCK_EPOCH (100k block) chunks, calling `gaugeController.gauge_relative_weight_write` each iteration. If a market is not updated for a long period (e.g., low activity or a whitelisted market with no deposits), the loop can run for many iterations, and each iteration performs external calls and storage writes. An attacker can also cause this by depositing a tiny amount into a market, then waiting, or by ensuring `lastRewardBlock` stays far behind via a market with zero supply (the `if (marketSupply > 0)` guard skips the loop but leaves `lastRewardBlock` unadvanced only when supply is zero — once supply becomes positive after a long gap, the loop runs from the stale `lastRewardBlock`).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker waits (or induces) a long gap where a whitelisted market has zero supply so `lastRewardBlock` is not advanced. 2) Attacker deposits a minimal amount via the market/gauge, making `marketSupply > 0`. 3) Next `update_market` call (triggered by `sync_ledger` or `claim`) loops from the stale `lastRewardBlock` to `block.number`, potentially thousands of iterations, each with an external call to `gauge_relative_weight_write` (which itself loops up to 500 weeks).
hypotheses.impact: `update_market` reverts out-of-gas, blocking `sync_ledger` and `claim` for that market — users cannot withdraw or claim rewards, funds effectively frozen.
hypotheses.recommendation: Cap iterations per call and allow incremental catch-up, or advance `lastRewardBlock` even when supply is zero.

hypotheses.title: Double-counting of delegated voting power via increaseAmount on delegated lock
hypotheses.description: When a user has delegated their lock to a delegatee, calling increaseAmount() adds the new value to the delegatee's `delegated` balance (via `newLocked.delegated += _value`) while the caller's own lock also retains its full `amount`. The caller's `delegated` field is not reduced, so the same CANTO contributes voting power to both the caller's lock and the delegatee's lock. This inflates total delegated voting power beyond the actual CANTO deposited.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker creates a lock and delegates to a colluding delegatee. 2) Attacker calls increaseAmount() with additional CANTO. 3) The delegatee's `delegated` is increased by the new amount, but the attacker's own `delegated` still reflects the original amount. 4) Both locks now report voting power derived from the same underlying CANTO, and the attacker can vote with inflated weight in GaugeController.
hypotheses.impact: Voting power inflation in GaugeController, allowing the attacker to capture a disproportionate share of CANTO emissions from LendingLedger, draining rewards from honest LPs.
hypotheses.recommendation: When increasing a delegated lock, subtract the added amount from the caller's `delegated` field (or track delegation ownership separately) so total delegated power never exceeds total locked CANTO.

hypotheses.title: LendingLedger.update_market uses current block.number for epochTime
hypotheses.description: Inside the while loop over blocks, epochTime is computed as referenceBlockTime + ((block.number - referenceBlockNumber) * averageBlockTime) / 1000, using the current block.number rather than the loop index i. This means every iteration of the loop uses the same epochTime (the current one), so gauge_relative_weight_write is queried for the current epoch's weight for all historical epochs being processed. Rewards for past epochs are therefore computed with the wrong (current) gauge weight, misallocating CANTO across markets.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes that a market's gauge weight has changed recently. 2) Attacker triggers update_market on a market whose lastRewardBlock is far in the past, causing all historical epochs to be weighted with the current gauge weight. 3) Attacker (or an accomplice market) with a currently high gauge weight receives disproportionately more rewards for past epochs than deserved.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect reward distribution across markets; some markets overpaid, others underpaid; potential drain of CANTO rewards.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute epochTime from the loop index i (e.g., referenceBlockTime + ((i - referenceBlockNumber) * averageBlockTime) / 1000) so each epoch uses its own timestamp.

hypotheses.title: LendingLedger.sync_ledger trusts msg.sender as lending market
hypotheses.description: sync_ledger() uses msg.sender as the lending market and only checks that it is whitelisted via update_market(). Any whitelisted market (or the LiquidityGauge mapped to it) can call sync_ledger with arbitrary _lender and _delta values, minting or burning user.amount and lendingMarketTotalBalance without any corresponding deposit/withdrawal. Since the ledger has no way to verify the delta against actual token movement, a malicious or buggy whitelisted market can inflate its own balance and drain CANTO rewards.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a contract that is whitelisted as a lending market (or compromises/uses an existing whitelisted market). 2) Attacker calls sync_ledger(victim, hugePositiveDelta) repeatedly to inflate lendingMarketTotalBalance and user.amount for chosen addresses. 3) Attacker calls claim() to withdraw CANTO rewards proportional to the inflated balance, draining the contract's CANTO balance.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of CANTO rewards held by LendingLedger; accounting corruption of user.amount and lendingMarketTotalBalance.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict sync_ledger to a trusted registry of markets and validate that _delta corresponds to actual token movements, or have the market pass a signed/verified delta.

hypotheses.title: LendingLedger.sync_ledger allows negative user.amount via unchecked cast
hypotheses.description: In the `_delta < 0` branch, `user.amount -= uint256(-_delta)` will revert on underflow (Solidity 0.8), which is safe. However, `user.rewardDebt -= int256((uint256(-_delta) * market.accCantoPerShare) / 1e18)` can underflow if `rewardDebt` is smaller than the computed value. This happens when a user withdraws more than they deposited relative to the current `accCantoPerShare`, or when `accCantoPerShare` has grown significantly since deposit. The subtraction is on `int256`, and Solidity 0.8 reverts on overflow/underflow, so this would revert — but the revert blocks legitimate withdrawals. More critically, `lendingMarketTotalBalance` is updated with `int256(lendingMarketTotalBalance[lendingMarket]) + _delta` and requires `>= 0`, but `user.amount` is not checked against `lendingMarketTotalBalance`, so a malicious market (whitelisted by governance) could call `sync_ledger` with arbitrary deltas to inflate `user.amount` without corresponding balance.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A whitelisted lending market (or the gauge) calls `sync_ledger(attacker, +hugeAmount)` without actually depositing. 2) `user.amount` is inflated, and `lendingMarketTotalBalance` is inflated. 3) Attacker calls `claim` to drain CANTO rewards proportional to the inflated amount. 4) Attacker calls `sync_ledger(attacker, -hugeAmount)` to reset, but the CANTO is already stolen.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of CANTO rewards from the LendingLedger contract; other users' rewards are diluted.
hypotheses.recommendation: Only allow `sync_ledger` to be called by the market itself with deltas that match actual token transfers, or verify the market's balance change.

hypotheses.title: update_market loop reads mutable gaugeController weight but writes accCantoPerShare; no reentrancy in gauge_relative_weight_write path
hypotheses.description: `update_market` calls `gaugeController.gauge_relative_weight_write(_market, epochTime)` inside its per-epoch loop, which mutates `points_weight`, `points_sum`, and `points_total` in GaugeController. This is an external non-view call inside a loop with `market.accCantoPerShare` updated immediately after. But `update_market` is NOT guarded by `nonReentrant`, and `gauge_relative_weight_write` calls `_get_weight`, `_get_total`, `_get_sum`, `_get_type_weight` — none make external calls so no direct reentrancy there. However, `claim()` calls `update_market` and then transfers CANTO — during which an attacker's `receive()` can call `update_market` again on a DIFFERENT market, reading the same GaugeController state while it is mid-loop-iteration for the first market. Read-only reentrancy of GaugeController state (points_total, time_total) can produce inconsistent weights for the second market while the first market's loop is not complete.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys contract with `receive()`. 2) Attacker calls `claim(marketA)` (requires prior sync). 3) `update_market(marketA)` runs its loop; on the external CANTO transfer, attacker's `receive()` calls `claim(marketB)` → `update_market(marketB)`. 4) If both markets share the same gauge type or total, the second computation reads `points_total`/`time_total` that may be duplicated-bumped, skewing weights. 5) Attacker repeats across markets in one tx.
hypotheses.impact: Skewed or duplicated reward accounting per market, potentially over- or under-counting CANTO owed and enabling reward extraction.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `nonReentrant` to `claim`, `update_market`, and `sync_ledger`, and reorder to write `market.lastRewardBlock` and `accCantoPerShare` before any external call.

hypotheses.title: LendingLedger.whiteListLendingMarket creates gauge without access control on gauge
hypotheses.description: whiteListLendingMarket() is onlyGovernance, but it deploys a new LiquidityGauge for the market. The gauge's depositUnderlying/withdrawUnderlying are callable by anyone, and _afterTokenTransfer calls sync_ledger. Since sync_ledger is unauthenticated, the gauge becomes an attack vector: any user can deposit underlying tokens into the gauge, receive gauge tokens, and then transfer them to manipulate the ledger. The gauge itself has no owner or pause mechanism.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Governance whitelists a market with _hasGauge = true. 2) Attacker deposits underlying tokens into the gauge, receiving gauge tokens. 3) Attacker transfers gauge tokens to another address, triggering sync_ledger with arbitrary amounts. 4) Attacker claims inflated rewards.
hypotheses.impact: Reward pool drained; incorrect market balances.
hypotheses.recommendation: Ensure sync_ledger is only callable by the gauge or market, and consider adding access control to gauge mint/burn paths.

hypotheses.title: GaugeController._gauge_relative_weight reads uninitialized points_total
hypotheses.description: `_gauge_relative_weight` reads `points_total[t]` where `t = (_time / WEEK) * WEEK`. If `points_total[t]` is zero (e.g., because `_get_total()` has not been called for that week, or because the gauge was added after the week started), the function returns 0. This means `gauge_relative_weight_write` can return 0 for a gauge that should have a non-zero weight, causing `LendingLedger.update_market` to compute `accCantoPerShare` with a zero weight and effectively skip reward accrual for that epoch. An attacker can exploit this by timing `sync_ledger` calls to coincide with uninitialized weeks.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes that `points_total[t]` is zero for the current week (e.g., because no one has called `checkpoint()` or `gauge_relative_weight_write` yet). 2) Attacker calls `LendingLedger.sync_ledger` (via a whitelisted market) to trigger `update_market`, which calls `gauge_relative_weight_write` and gets 0. 3) `accCantoPerShare` is not incremented for that block range. 4) Attacker then calls `checkpoint()` to initialize `points_total`, and subsequent `update_market` calls accrue rewards for the attacker's balance only.
hypotheses.impact: Reward misallocation; honest LPs lose rewards for the uninitialized period, attacker captures them.
hypotheses.recommendation: Ensure `_get_total()` is called before reading `points_total`, or revert if `points_total[t] == 0` in `_gauge_relative_weight`.

hypotheses.title: LiquidityGauge.withdrawUnderlying can be blocked by LendingLedger sync revert
hypotheses.description: `_afterTokenTransfer` calls `LendingLedger.sync_ledger(from, -amount)` on every burn/transfer. `sync_ledger` calls `update_market`, which can revert (out-of-gas, or `Market balance underflow` if accounting drifts, or if the market is de-whitelisted). Since `_burn` triggers `_afterTokenTransfer` before the underlying transfer, any revert in `sync_ledger` blocks the entire withdrawal, trapping user funds in the gauge.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (or any user) causes `lendingMarketTotalBalance` for the gauge's market to become inconsistent, or waits until `update_market`'s loop is too expensive. 2) When any user calls `withdrawUnderlying`, `_burn` → `_afterTokenTransfer` → `sync_ledger` reverts. 3) The withdrawal reverts, and the user's underlying tokens remain locked in the gauge.
hypotheses.impact: Users cannot withdraw underlying tokens from the gauge; funds frozen.
hypotheses.recommendation: Make `sync_ledger` failures non-blocking (try/catch) or decouple ledger sync from token transfers.

hypotheses.title: LiquidityGauge._afterTokenTransfer calls sync_ledger on every transfer, enabling griefing
hypotheses.description: `_afterTokenTransfer` calls `LendingLedger(lendingLedger).sync_ledger(from, -amount)` and `sync_ledger(to, amount)` on every token transfer, including mints and burns. If `sync_ledger` reverts (e.g., due to `update_market` failing, market not whitelisted, or underflow in `user.amount`), the entire transfer reverts. An attacker can transfer tokens to an address that causes `sync_ledger` to revert (e.g., if the recipient's `user.amount` would underflow on a subsequent transfer), effectively freezing the gauge token for that user. Additionally, the `from != address(0)` check means burns trigger `sync_ledger(from, -amount)`, which can underflow if the user's ledger amount is less than the burn amount.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deposits underlying tokens to get gauge tokens. 2) Attacker transfers gauge tokens to a victim or to a contract that cannot receive them (causing sync_ledger to revert). 3) The victim's gauge tokens become non-transferable, or the attacker can cause `withdrawUnderlying` to revert by manipulating ledger state via transfers.
hypotheses.impact: Gauge tokens can be frozen or rendered non-transferable, and users may be unable to withdraw their underlying tokens.
hypotheses.recommendation: Make `sync_ledger` failures non-fatal (try/catch) or ensure ledger state is always consistent with token balances; avoid calling sync_ledger on burns if the ledger amount may be less than the burn amount.

hypotheses.title: VotingEscrow.increaseAmount resets lock end without extending delegatee lock
hypotheses.description: When a user has delegated their lock (delegatee != msg.sender), increaseAmount updates the sender's lock end to _floorToWeek(block.timestamp + LOCKTIME) and checkpoints the sender, then updates the delegatee's delegated amount but does NOT extend the delegatee's lock end. The delegatee's lock may expire sooner than the sender's, so the sender's newly added voting power (delegated to the delegatee) can outlive the delegatee's lock. When the delegatee withdraws, the delegated amount is reduced by the delegatee's own amount only, leaving the sender's delegated contribution stranded and the sender unable to withdraw until their own lock expires.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (delegatee) accepts delegation from a victim. 2) Victim calls increaseAmount, extending their lock end but not the delegatee's. 3) Delegatee waits until their own lock expires and calls withdraw, removing their own amount from delegated but leaving the victim's delegated amount in the delegatee's lock. 4) The delegatee's lock now has delegated > 0 but amount == 0, and the victim's funds are effectively locked until the victim's own lock expires; meanwhile the delegatee's voting power accounting is corrupted.
hypotheses.impact: Frozen funds for the victim; inconsistent delegated/amount state; potential loss of voting power accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: When increasing a delegated lock, also extend the delegatee's lock end to match, or disallow increaseAmount on delegated locks.

hypotheses.title: LiquidityGauge double-counts deposits via sync_ledger on mint and transfer
hypotheses.description: `_afterTokenTransfer` calls `sync_ledger(from, -amount)` and `sync_ledger(to, +amount)` on every transfer, including the mint path where `from == address(0)` is skipped but `to` is credited. However, `depositUnderlying` mints to the user, which credits the ledger once, and any subsequent transfer between users moves the credit correctly. The real issue is that `withdrawUnderlying` burns from the user, which triggers `sync_ledger(user, -amount)` — but the user's ledger `amount` was already credited at deposit. This is consistent. The actual double-count arises because `LendingLedger.sync_ledger` is called with `msg.sender == liquidityGauge`, and inside it re-maps `lendingMarket = liquidityGauges[lendingMarket]` to the underlying market. Since `liquidityGauges` is a two-way mapping, when the gauge calls sync_ledger, `lendingMarket` becomes the underlying market, and `userInfo[market][user]` is updated. But the gauge's own ERC20 balance is not tracked in the ledger — only the user's. So a user can deposit into the gauge (credited), then transfer gauge tokens to another address (credited to recipient, debited from sender), and the recipient can withdraw underlying directly from the gauge without ever having deposited — the ledger accounting follows the gauge token, which is correct. The flaw is that `depositUnderlying` mints gauge tokens AND the ledger credits the user, but the gauge contract itself holds the underlying; if a user transfers gauge tokens to the gauge contract itself (or to address(0) via burn), the ledger is debited but the underlying stays in the gauge, allowing the remaining holders to withdraw more than their share.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deposits X underlying, receives X gauge tokens, ledger credits X. 2) Attacker transfers gauge tokens to the gauge contract address itself (or burns them via `burn`), triggering `sync_ledger(attacker, -X)` which debits the ledger. 3) The underlying X remains in the gauge contract. 4) Attacker (or another holder) withdraws underlying using remaining gauge tokens, draining the orphaned X.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of funds — underlying tokens become claimable by other gauge holders, and the ledger's `lendingMarketTotalBalance` no longer matches real holdings.
hypotheses.recommendation: Prevent transfers to the gauge contract itself and to address(0) via burn, or reconcile the ledger against actual underlying balance held by the gauge.

hypotheses.title: VotingEscrow.withdraw sends CANTO before state is fully settled
hypotheses.description: `withdraw()` updates `locked[msg.sender]` and calls `_checkpoint` before sending CANTO via `msg.sender.call{value: amountToSend}("")`. While `nonReentrant` is present, the external call to `msg.sender` can still invoke other contracts (e.g., a malicious `receive()` that calls `GaugeController.vote_for_gauge_weights` or `LendingLedger.sync_ledger`). Because `_checkpoint` has already zeroed the user's lock, the re-entrant call sees a zero lock, but the attacker can use the re-entrancy to manipulate gauge weights or ledger state in the same transaction before the CANTO transfer is finalized.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker creates a lock and votes on a gauge. 2) Attacker calls `withdraw()` after lock expiry. 3) During the CANTO `call`, attacker's `receive()` calls `GaugeController.vote_for_gauge_weights` with a stale slope (see separate finding) or `LendingLedger.sync_ledger` to manipulate accounting. 4) The re-entrant call executes with the attacker's lock already zeroed, but the attacker can still influence gauge/ledger state.
hypotheses.impact: Gauge weight manipulation or ledger accounting corruption in the same transaction as a withdrawal.
hypotheses.recommendation: Follow checks-effects-interactions strictly and consider a pull-pattern for CANTO withdrawals, or add reentrancy guards to GaugeController and LendingLedger entry points.

hypotheses.title: LendingLedger.update_market uses stale gauge_relative_weight_write
hypotheses.description: `update_market` calls `gaugeController.gauge_relative_weight_write(_market, epochTime)` inside a loop over blocks. `gauge_relative_weight_write` calls `_get_weight` and `_get_total`, which fill historical points up to `block.timestamp`, but the `_time` argument passed is `epochTime` (derived from block number). If `epochTime` is in the past relative to the last checkpoint, the function returns the weight for that past week, which may not reflect the current gauge weight. An attacker can exploit this by manipulating `epochTime` (see separate finding) or by timing calls to read a stale weight.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker waits until `epochTime` falls in a week where the gauge weight was high. 2) Attacker calls `sync_ledger` to trigger `update_market`, which reads the high weight. 3) `accCantoPerShare` is inflated for the attacker's balance. 4) Attacker claims rewards at the inflated rate.
hypotheses.impact: Reward inflation; attacker extracts more CANTO than entitled.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `block.timestamp` for the weight lookup, or ensure `epochTime` is always current.

hypotheses.title: withdraw() external call to msg.sender after state update is safe, but unlockOverride allows non-expired drainage
hypotheses.description: `withdraw()` correctly updates `locked[msg.sender]` and calls `_checkpoint` before the native transfer, and is protected by `nonReentrant`. However, when `unlockOverride` is enabled by governance, any user can withdraw an entire unexpired lock immediately, which combined with the fixed 5-year lock RESET in `createLock/increaseAmount` means the veCANTO voting power is not actually locked. This is an ordering/invariant violation (state says 5-year lock, but withdrawal can occur any time).
hypotheses.attackPath: Not directly exploitable by an untrusted actor without `unlockOverride == true`; only governance can flip it. Reported as informational ordering risk.
hypotheses.impact: If governance flips override (migration path), all locks can be exited before their intended end date, undermining gauge voting weight and rewards math.
hypotheses.recommendation: When `unlockOverride` is toggled, also zero out voting power or emit an event cleared with each affected user's checkpoint.

hypotheses.title: GaugeController vote_for_gauge_weights can be griefed via unbounded slope changes
hypotheses.description: The `_get_total()` function iterates over all gauge types and up to 500 weeks per type, and `_get_weight`/`_get_sum`/`_get_type_weight` each loop up to 500 iterations. Any user can call `vote_for_gauge_weights` repeatedly with tiny weights to force `_get_total()` to run, and as `n_gauge_types` grows (governance-controlled but each type adds a nested loop), the gas cost of `_get_total()` grows multiplicatively. More critically, `_get_total()` is invoked on every vote, and the inner loop over `n_gauge_types` combined with the 500-week loop can exceed block gas limits, bricking voting and thus `gauge_relative_weight_write` used by LendingLedger.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker repeatedly calls `vote_for_gauge_weights` on any gauge with weight 0 or 1 to trigger `_get_total()`. 2) Each call advances `time_total` and forces the 500-iteration loop. 3) As more gauge types are added, the nested loop cost grows; eventually calls revert out-of-gas, blocking all voting and `gauge_relative_weight_write` calls from `LendingLedger.update_market`.
hypotheses.impact: Voting and reward-weight updates become uncallable; LendingLedger.update_market reverts, freezing reward accrual and blocking sync_ledger/claim flows.
hypotheses.recommendation: Bound the number of gauge types and/or cap the week-fill loop iterations, and allow partial checkpointing so a single call cannot exceed block gas.

hypotheses.title: VotingEscrow.withdraw lacks nonReentrant protection on CANTO send
hypotheses.description: `withdraw()` is marked `nonReentrant`, but the `_checkpoint` call and the subsequent `msg.sender.call{value: amountToSend}("")` occur after state updates. However, the `nonReentrant` modifier only protects against re-entering `withdraw` itself; the attacker can re-enter `createLock` or `increaseAmount` (which are also `nonReentrant`) — actually those are guarded. The real issue: `withdraw()` sets `newLocked.delegated -= int128(int256(amountToSend))` and then sets `newLocked.delegated = 0` before checkpointing, but the checkpoint uses `newLocked` with `delegated = 0` while `locked[msg.sender]` was already stored with the non-zero delegated value. This inconsistency between stored state and checkpointed state can be exploited across multiple withdrawals or combined with delegation to mis-account voting power.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker creates a lock and delegates to a delegatee. 2) Attacker calls `withdraw()` after lock expiry. 3) The stored `locked[msg.sender]` retains `delegated` value while checkpoint uses zeroed `delegated`, causing slope/bias accounting mismatch. 4) Attacker repeats or combines with `increaseAmount` to accumulate incorrect voting power in GaugeController.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect voting power accounting in GaugeController, allowing disproportionate gauge weight votes and misallocation of CANTO rewards.
hypotheses.recommendation: Ensure `locked[msg.sender]` and the checkpointed `newLocked` are consistent; zero out `delegated` in the stored struct before checkpointing.

hypotheses.title: secRewardsPerShare accrues without any secondary reward funding
hypotheses.description: `market.secRewardsPerShare += uint128((blockDelta * 1e36) / marketSupply)` accrues secondary rewards per share unconditionally, but there is no corresponding funding mechanism, no `secRewards` token transfer, and no claim path for secondary rewards in this contract. The accumulator grows unboundedly and is stored in `user.secRewardDebt`, but no code ever pays it out. If a future claim path is added or if this value is used elsewhere, the contract has no funds backing it.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not directly exploitable by an untrusted actor in the current code, but any future integration or off-chain accounting that trusts `secRewardsPerShare` will be misled. Additionally, the unbounded growth of `secRewardsPerShare` combined with `user.secRewardDebt` accumulation can overflow int256/uint128 in extreme cases, corrupting user state.
hypotheses.impact: Phantom liabilities; potential overflow of `secRewardsPerShare` (uint128) or `secRewardDebt` (int256) causing accounting corruption and blocking sync_ledger/claim.
hypotheses.recommendation: Either remove the secondary reward accumulator entirely, or gate it behind an actual funded secondary reward token with a matching claim path.

hypotheses.title: LendingLedger.claim does not update secRewardDebt
hypotheses.description: claim() updates user.rewardDebt to accumulatedCanto but never updates user.secRewardDebt. The secondary rewards accumulator (secRewardsPerShare) is tracked in sync_ledger, but claim() does not settle or reset secRewardDebt. As a result, secondary rewards are never actually claimable through this function, and the secRewardDebt value drifts relative to the market's secRewardsPerShare, causing incorrect accounting if a future claim path is added or if the value is used elsewhere.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Users deposit into a market, accruing secRewardDebt via sync_ledger. 2) Users call claim() to receive CANTO; secRewardDebt is left unchanged. 3) If any future logic or external integration relies on secRewardDebt, it will be stale and inconsistent with the market's secRewardsPerShare, potentially allowing double-claiming or blocking claims.
hypotheses.impact: Secondary rewards are effectively frozen; accounting inconsistency between user.secRewardDebt and market.secRewardsPerShare.
hypotheses.recommendation: In claim(), also compute and settle secondary rewards (or explicitly document that secRewardDebt is unused and remove it).

hypotheses.title: VotingEscrow.withdraw allows withdrawal when unlockOverride is true by governance
hypotheses.description: withdraw() checks require(locked_.end <= block.timestamp || unlockOverride, "Lock not expired"). The unlockOverride flag is toggled by governance via toggleUnlockOverride(). While governance is trusted, the flag is a global switch that, once enabled, allows any user to withdraw their lock early. This is intended, but the flag is not scoped and can be left on, enabling premature withdrawals that break voting power accounting in GaugeController and LendingLedger.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Governance toggles unlockOverride (trusted action). 2) Any user calls withdraw() before lock expiry. 3) Voting power is removed early, but GaugeController may still have recorded votes based on the old lock end.
hypotheses.impact: Voting power and gauge weight accounting become inconsistent; users can exit locks early, potentially manipulating votes.
hypotheses.recommendation: Scope the override to specific users or require governance to explicitly authorize each early withdrawal; or ensure GaugeController is notified when locks are withdrawn early.

hypotheses.title: VotingEscrow._checkpoint slopeChanges overwrite loses prior scheduled changes
hypotheses.description: In `_checkpoint`, when `_newLocked.end == _oldLocked.end`, the code sets `oldSlopeDelta = oldSlopeDelta - userNewPoint.slope` and writes `slopeChanges[_oldLocked.end] = oldSlopeDelta`. But `oldSlopeDelta` was read as `slopeChanges[_oldLocked.end]` at the start, which already includes the user's old slope. The logic adds `userOldPoint.slope` then subtracts `userNewPoint.slope`, which is correct for the user's own contribution. However, if multiple users share the same `end` timestamp, the `slopeChanges` mapping is a single value per timestamp — the code correctly accumulates across users. The bug is that when `_newLocked.end > _oldLocked.end`, the code writes `slopeChanges[_newLocked.end] = newSlopeDelta` where `newSlopeDelta = slopeChanges[_newLocked.end] - userNewPoint.slope`. If `slopeChanges[_newLocked.end]` was 0 (no prior changes), this becomes `-userNewPoint.slope`, which is a negative value stored in an `int128` — correct. But if another user later extends to the same `end`, the accumulation works. The real issue: when `_oldLocked.end > block.timestamp` and `_newLocked.end == _oldLocked.end`, the code writes `slopeChanges[_oldLocked.end] = oldSlopeDelta` but does NOT also update `slopeChanges[_newLocked.end]` (same value), which is fine. However, if `_newLocked.end > _oldLocked.end`, the old slope change at `_oldLocked.end` is updated, but the new slope change at `_newLocked.end` is set to `newSlopeDelta` which was read BEFORE the old slope was added — this can cause the new end's slope change to be incorrect if there were prior changes at that timestamp.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User A locks with end T1. 2) User B locks with end T2 > T1. 3) User A extends to T2. 4) The `slopeChanges[T2]` is computed as `slopeChanges[T2] - userNewPoint.slope`, but `slopeChanges[T2]` was read before User A's old slope was removed from T1. If User B's slope change at T2 was already recorded, it's preserved. The bug manifests when `newSlopeDelta` is read as 0 (no prior changes at T2) but there actually were changes that were overwritten by a previous checkpoint in the same block.
hypotheses.impact: Global slope accounting drifts from actual sum of user slopes, causing `totalSupply` to be incorrect and rewards to be misallocated.
hypotheses.recommendation: Re-read `slopeChanges[_newLocked.end]` after updating `slopeChanges[_oldLocked.end]` to ensure consistency.

hypotheses.title: sync_ledger trusts arbitrary caller address; no whitelist of caller even though comment implies gauge
hypotheses.description: `sync_ledger` accepts `_lender` and `_delta` with `msg.sender` used as `lendingMarket`, only requiring `liquidityGauges[lendingMarket] != address(0)` to remap to the real market. For markets WITHOUT a liquidity gauge, `liquidityGauges[market] == address(0)`, so `lendingMarket = msg.sender` and any whitelisted market (contract) can call. But `sync_ledger` is externally callable — any EOA can call it if it happens to be the market address? No — msg.sender must equal a whitelisted market. Since msg.sender is the EOA, it's not whitelisted → fails `update_market` require. However, for markets WITH gauges, the gauge address is whitelisted via `liquidityGauges` reverse mapping; but the reverse mapping `liquidityGauges[gauge] = market` is set, so an attacker cannot spoof this. Still, the trust of caller is implicit — if any whitelisted market contract is itself attacker-deployed via governance whitelisting, it can arbitrarily credit `_lender` amounts and inflate `lendingMarketTotalBalance`.
hypotheses.attackPath: Untrusted actor cannot trigger directly; requires a whitelisted market to be malicious. Under lens scope only: the ordering of `update_market` before `user.amount` update is correct, but `sync_ledger` does not validate the caller is a gauge or market contract via explicit check. Marked lower confidence.
hypotheses.impact: Potential credit-mint accounting inflation if a whitelisted contract is malicious or has a bug; not directly reachable by an outsider.
hypotheses.recommendation: Explicitly validate `msg.sender == liquidityGauge` when a gauge exists, and require direct ledger callers to have their ledger-credit tracked.

hypotheses.title: votingEscrow.balanceOfAt block estimate can be gamed by sandwich around checkpoint
hypotheses.description: `balanceOfAt` interpolates the block timestamp using `pointHistory[epoch]` and `pointHistory[epoch+1]`, but the interpolated `blockTime` uses `block.number - point0.blk` and `block.timestamp - point0.ts` when `epoch == maxEpoch`. In the same block a user checkpoints (createLock, withdraw, etc.), the current epoch point has `blk = block.number` and `ts = block.timestamp`, so queries against that block can produce drift. Moreover, `_findUserBlockEpoch` can return the current user point, whose bias is extrapolated using `blockTime` split between two points with potentially equal `blk`.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker can cause a user's `balanceOfAt` on the same block as a checkpoint to return inflated/deflated bias by forcing the checkpoint in the same block via a large deposit/increaseAmount, then reading cross-contract (GaugeController votes) in the same transaction, exploiting the mismatch between `point.blk` and interpolated time.
hypotheses.impact: Voting power mis-estimated at historical block reads; not directly exploitable for funds but can mislead external integrators reading weight.
hypotheses.recommendation: Interpolation should fall back to using `point0.ts` when `dBlock == 0` and reject same-block queries or use the last epoch strictly before the requested block.

hypotheses.title: VotingEscrow.createLock and increaseAmount lack deadline/nonce, but no signature scheme exists
hypotheses.description: The contract does not implement any signature-based meta-transaction or permit functionality, so there is no missing nonce/deadline/chain-id issue in the traditional sense. However, the audit lens requires checking for signature replay; since no signatures are used, this is not exploitable. This finding is included only to note the absence of signature-based entry points, which is not a vulnerability.
hypotheses.attackPath: N/A — no signature-based functions exist.
hypotheses.impact: None.
hypotheses.recommendation: No action needed; if meta-transactions are added later, include nonce, deadline, chainId, and verifying contract address.

hypotheses.title: LendingLedger.claim uses call and can be griefed by reverting receiver
hypotheses.description: `claim` sends CANTO via `msg.sender.call{value: cantoToSend}("")` and requires success. A contract that reverts on receive can only block its own claim, so this is self-griefing and not a real DoS for others. However, if `cantoToSend` is zero, the call is still made with zero value; some contracts revert on zero-value calls, but again only affects the caller. Not a cross-user DoS.
hypotheses.attackPath: N/A — only the caller is affected.
hypotheses.impact: Self-only; no cross-user impact.
hypotheses.recommendation: Skip the call when `cantoToSend == 0`.
